narrative:
The model estimated an 82% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a high-risk estimate, not a certainty, but it was strong enough that your law school application was denied. This decision was not based on your gender or race.

The strongest reason was your third-year class standing. You were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile. That very low ranking was the top factor pushing the prediction toward bar failure. The second most influential factor was your LSAT score: 26, compared with an accepted-student average of about 37. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.80, below the accepted average of 3.23, was the third most important factor. Notably, its influence was smaller and leaned slightly toward passing rather than failing; it did not drive the rejection as strongly as your class standing or LSAT.

To move forward, ask admissions for feedback and identify whether any deficiencies can be addressed. Consider focused LSAT preparation and a retake, additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate record showing stronger academic performance, and an explanatory addendum if there are circumstances behind your record. Reapply when you can present stronger evidence of bar-readiness, and consider schools that review applicants more holistically.
